atoms.text: In the 16th and 17th century, Protestant English monarchs colonised Catholic Ireland. The so-called plantations of Ireland involved confiscating Irish-owned land and distributing it amongst settlers from Great Britain.

atoms.a: What religion did most Irish people identify with?

atoms.text: The biggest plantation was in the traditional Irish province Ulster in the North, where six out of nine counties were confiscated. The settlement of Scottish and Northern English protestants created a separate and lasting Protestant community in Ulster with strong ties to Great Britain.

b: A majority of Catholics in Ulster

atoms.text: Ireland lost its independence in 1801. However, calls for Home Rule and growing Irish nationalism led to the partition of Ireland in 1921. Six former Ulster counties formed the predominantly Protestant Northern Ireland. The rest became the mostly Catholic Irish Free State (later Republic of Ireland).

atoms.a: Which were the two states established by the partition?

atoms.b: Whilst Ireland is and was predominantly ((Catholic)), the British settlers formed a new Protestant minority.
Many Catholics defined themselves as ((Irish)) (and not as British). It was their aim to be united with the ((Republic_of_Ireland)).

With the Ulster Plantation Protestant settlers were given land in the ((northern)) part of Ireland. The foreign landowners constituted a new upper class, whereas most Catholics were financially ((underprivileged)).
The long-existing ((++conflict friendship union)) escalated in 1968 and British troops were sent to Northern Ireland to restore order.

On the so-called “Bloody Sunday” in 1972, British ((++soldiers kings politicians)) shot 13 unarmed protestors in Derry (Londonderry). This caused three decades of violent conflict, killing more than 3,500 people.
During this time the Northern Ireland Government was ((++suspended powerful quiet)) and the country came under “direct rule” from Westminster.

Finally, in 1998 the Good Friday Agreement led to disarmament and a division of governmental power, although a ((++devolved dependent English)) Northern Irish government did not come into existence until 2007.

atoms.text: While the political situation following the Good Friday Agreement was relatively stable, a split still remained in Northern Ireland's society. In Belfast, a so-called peace wall divides predominately loyalist and nationalist neighbourhoods.
atoms.sound: While the political situation following the Good Friday Agreement was relatively stable, a split still remained in Northern Ireland's society. In Belfast, a so-called peace wall divides predominately loyalist and nationalist neighbourhoods.

atoms.a: After the Good Friday Agreement, the conflict was fully solved.

atoms.text: In the Brexit referendum of 2016, 55.78 % of Northern Irish voted to remain part of the EU. The Brexit treaty imposed new Irish Sea Borders with the rest of the UK, resulting in unrest among the loyalist groups. Politically, in 2024, a nationalist from Sinn Féin was appointed First Minister for the very first time.
